system: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses
primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
mechanism: Narcolepsy type 1 is characterized by loss of hypocretin (orexin)-producing neurons in the lateral hypothalamus. Orexin normally stabilizes wake-promoting networks and helps maintain separation between wakefulness and REM sleep. Deficiency destabilizes sleep-wake transitions and permits REM-associated phenomena such as cataplexy, sleep paralysis, and hypnagogic hallucinations to intrude into wakefulness.
vignette: A 19-year-old college student has recurrent irresistible episodes of daytime sleep despite adequate time in bed. She sometimes awakens unable to move for several seconds and has vivid dreamlike images as she falls asleep. On several occasions, laughing with friends has caused sudden buckling of her knees while she remained fully conscious.
lead: Which of the following changes in the central nervous system most directly underlies this patient's disorder?
correct: Loss of orexin-producing neurons in the lateral hypothalamus
distractors: Degeneration of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta
Loss of cholinergic neurons in the nucleus basalis of Meynert
Immune-mediated destruction of central nervous system myelin
Degeneration of anterior horn motor neurons
distractor_notes: Substantia nigra pars compacta dopaminergic degeneration is the characteristic mechanism of Parkinson disease and produces bradykinesia, rigidity, and resting tremor rather than sleep attacks with cataplexy.
Loss of cholinergic neurons in the nucleus basalis of Meynert is associated with Alzheimer disease and progressive cognitive decline, not the REM-intrusion syndrome shown here.

Immune-mediated CNS demyelination is characteristic of multiple sclerosis and produces focal neurologic deficits disseminated in time and space rather than emotion-triggered cataplexy and irresistible daytime sleep.
Anterior horn motor-neuron degeneration causes lower motor neuron weakness and atrophy, as in motor neuron disorders, and does not explain the sleep-wake/REM phenomena in this patient.
key_expl: This patient has narcolepsy type 1: excessive daytime sleepiness together with cataplexy, sleep paralysis, and hypnagogic hallucinations. MedlinePlus and NCBI describe loss of hypocretin/orexin-producing hypothalamic neurons as the central abnormality in narcolepsy with cataplexy. Orexin normally supports stable wakefulness; when this system is deficient, transitions between wake and sleep become unstable and REM-related atonia and dream phenomena can intrude into wakefulness.
objective: Explain narcolepsy type 1 as loss of orexin/hypocretin-producing neurons in the lateral hypothalamus, causing unstable sleep-wake transitions and intrusion of REM phenomena into wakefulness.

sources.title: Narcolepsy — StatPearls
sources.support: NCBI describes narcolepsy type 1 as loss of orexin/hypocretin-containing neurons and explains that orexin deficiency destabilizes sleep-wake boundaries, permitting REM-related phenomena.

sources.title: Narcolepsy — MedlinePlus Genetics
sources.support: MedlinePlus describes excessive daytime sleepiness, cataplexy, sleep paralysis, and hallucinations and explains that narcolepsy with cataplexy commonly involves loss of hypothalamic hypocretin-producing neurons.

sources.title: Parkinson Disease — StatPearls
sources.support: NCBI describes degeneration of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta as a central feature of Parkinson disease.

sources.title: Alzheimer Disease — StatPearls
sources.support: NCBI describes degeneration of cholinergic neurons, including the nucleus basalis of Meynert, in Alzheimer disease.

sources.title: Multiple Sclerosis — StatPearls
sources.support: NCBI describes multiple sclerosis as immune-mediated inflammatory demyelination of the central nervous system.
